newsitem.title: USA: Chip-making equipment makers agree to new standards.
newsitem.headline: Chip-making equipment makers agree to new standards.

text.p: The semiconductor equipment industry is expected to unveil guidelines on Wednesday that will set worldwide standards for handling a new type of raw material for making computer chips.

The new guidelines will help the industry more quickly switch to the manufacture of 300-millimeter silicon wafers, the round slabs of semiconductor material from which almost all computer chips are made, industry executives said.

"You're going to end up with global standards, instead of one for U.S., one for Japan and one for Europe," said Stan Myers, president of Semiconductor Equipment and Materials International, the industry's main trade group. "There has to be collaboration, otherwise the costs would be out of sight."

Currently, most chip-making equipment is designed to handle 200-millimeter wafers. The bigger 300-millimeter wafer will allow semiconductor companies like Intel Corp. and Texas Instruments Inc. to double the number of chips they make in one batch.
The switch from 200- to 300-millimeter wafers is expected to cost chipmakers $14 billion in new semiconductor processing machinery and factories, according to SEMI.
The move, however, is expected to cut manufacturing costs by as much as 20 percent to 30 percent.

Dozens of manufacturing steps and devices are used to make wafers. The industry has to insure that the processing equipment, which is manufactured by several companies around the world, can handle the same wafer size and manufacturing methodology.
The guidelines were drawn up by American, Japanese and European trade groups and semiconductor equipment makers, such as Applied Materials Inc. and Novellus Systems Inc.
They will be presented at this week's Semicon West in San Francisco, a semiconducter industry trade show.
Companies such as Applied Materials, Novellus and Lam Research Corp. will preview 300-millimeter wafer processing machinery at the show.
